Apple Unveils First MacBook Pro with a Touchscreen and OLED Display

On October 28, 2026, at its "Pro and Tell" event in Los Angeles, Apple announced new MacBook Pro models featuring a PROLED XDR display. These are the first Mac laptops to support touch input and utilize a tandem OLED screen. The 14-inch model starts at $2,899 (with the M5 Pro chip), while the 16-inch model begins at $3,399 (also with the M5 Pro). Configurations featuring the M5 Max chip start at $4,499 and $4,799, respectively. Pre-orders open on October 28, with shipments beginning November 6.

The display offers brightness of up to 2,000 nits (for both HDR and SDR content), a contrast ratio of 10,000,000:1, and an adaptive refresh rate ranging from 10 Hz to 120 Hz (ProMotion). The touch sensor is integrated directly into the display panel. New features include the "Dynamic Island," an illuminated Apple logo on the lid, and a lighter chassis (the 14-inch model weighs approximately 1.36 kg). The devices are powered by the same M5 Pro and M5 Max chips found in previous models, supporting up to 128 GB of RAM and up to 16 TB of storage. They are available in Space Black and Silver, with an optional nano-texture glass finish.

In the days leading up to the event, Apple also introduced an updated iPad mini (8th generation), featuring an 8.5-inch OLED display, the A20 Pro chip, a thinner 5.4 mm chassis, IP67-rated protection, and a new speaker system. The starting price is $699 (for the Wi-Fi model with 128 GB of storage). In addition, a 14-inch MacBook Pro and an iMac powered by the M6 ​​chip were announced (with starting prices of $1,999 and $1,499, respectively). These devices will go on sale during the same timeframe.

📌 Atomic Swaps: Exchanging Crypto Without Trusting an Intermediary

Main Points
⏺ Atomic swaps allow participants to exchange assets without handing funds to a centralized custodian
⏺ The mechanism is designed so both sides receive their assets or the exchange doesn't complete
⏺ This post explains why atomic swaps are an interesting approach to decentralized trading

1️⃣ Core Idea — two users want to exchange assets from different blockchains without trusting an exchange or intermediary with their funds.
2️⃣ How It Works — one approach uses cryptographic secrets and time restrictions to coordinate an exchange under predefined rules.
3️⃣ Main Advantage — participants don't need to transfer custody of their assets to a third party during the exchange.
4️⃣ The Challenges — networks need compatible mechanisms, while participants need liquidity, time, and correct execution.
5️⃣ Practical Rule — before swapping, review fees on both chains, lock periods, technical requirements, and refund conditions.

Final Thoughts

Atomic swaps aim to solve a fundamental crypto problem: how to exchange value with a stranger without relying on their honesty.

A Letter to America, From a Frenchman Who Loves You

Yesterday, the Prime Minister of Poland posted this: "Restoring the rule of law is our duty. After years of PiS-led lawlessness, this is a difficult process, sometimes painful, and it requires decisive action. There is no other way."

Read it slowly. "There is no other way." In today's Europe, that is the sentence a government says right before doing something it could not do through the normal rules.

I'm French. I'm the grandson of a farmer from Brittany. I taught myself to code at twelve, spent a year in Silicon Valley when I was young, and today I build a tech company between Paris and San Francisco. I'm writing to you because I watch what is happening to my continent, and I'm afraid you are about to take the same road.

Let me tell you what "rule of law" means in Europe now.

When Donald Tusk came to power in December 2023, one of his first moves was to take over Poland's public broadcaster. Rather than pass a media law the president would veto, his government used corporate law to replace its leadership, and the state news channel briefly went dark. When that was blocked, it put public TV into liquidation. When the Constitutional Tribunal ruled against the government, the government stopped recognizing its rulings. Tusk himself said openly that restoring the rule of law would sometimes require decisions that would not fully meet the criteria of legality.

And Brussels? For years, the European Commission froze billions in EU funds to Poland over "rule of law" concerns under the previous conservative government. Once Tusk was in, it unfroze the money and closed its proceedings.

That's the lesson. In Europe, the rule of law is no longer a principle. It is a label. When a conservative government reshapes the courts, it's an assault on democracy. When a pro-Brussels government ignores a court, it's "restoring the rule of law."

It isn't only Poland. In Romania in December 2024, the Constitutional Court annulled the first round of a presidential election after the wrong candidate came first. In France, a TV channel, C8, lost its broadcasting license in 2025, and this week a member of parliament declared that shutting down CNEWS, the most-watched news channel in the country, is "a priority." In Germany, domestic intelligence labeled the main opposition party extremist. The GOP Wants Gen Z Men. Gen Z Men Aren’t Buying It


The Republican Party is looking for its next generation of voters. But a campaign aimed at one of the most traditionally conservative corners of American college life is revealing an uncomfortable reality: young men are not necessarily interested in becoming the party’s political lifeline.

Conservative activist CJ Pearson has taken his message directly to college campuses, hoping to reconnect young men with the GOP ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. 

Through his Make America Party Again PAC, Pearson has been organizing tailgate events around college football games, handing out campaign merchandise and trying to turn campus enthusiasm into political engagement.

One of his stops was the University of Alabama, where he appeared alongside popular football superfan Roll Tide Willie. The setting seemed ideal for a Republican outreach campaign. College football, fraternity culture and conservative politics have long been associated with one another in parts of the South.

But the response was far less enthusiastic than organizers might have hoped.

Some fraternity members treated the political merchandise as a joke. Others described themselves as politically disengaged or simply refused to discuss their views. For many students, politics has become increasingly divisive, while voting itself seems disconnected from their everyday concerns.

Others were more willing to engage but offered a message Republicans may find difficult to hear. One student argued that the party needs to move away from its more confrontational approach and appeal to voters closer to the political center.

That is precisely the challenge facing the GOP. The party has invested heavily in attracting young male voters, a demographic that helped Donald Trump build his political coalition. Yet the appeal of the MAGA brand is no longer universal among younger Americans, particularly those who are uncomfortable with the current political climate.

Pearson believes the problem cannot be solved through occasional appearances and campaign giveaways. Reaching young voters, he argues, requires consistent engagement and personal relationships. His team also points out that conservative sentiment remains strong on many campuses, even among students who are not registered to vote or do not participate in elections.

The broader problem is turnout. Having sympathizers is one thing. Convincing them to show up at the polls is another.

The Alabama event also unfolded against the backdrop of controversy surrounding the fraternity hosting it, including disciplinary action over hazing allegations. That added another layer of complexity to an already carefully staged political appearance.

Perhaps the most revealing moment came afterward. Roll Tide Willie, who had encouraged students to exercise their right to vote, later posted online that voting was a waste of time and complained about the flood of election-related mail.

For Republicans, the episode captures a difficult political reality. Winning young men's attention does not automatically translate into winning their loyalty. And in a generation increasingly skeptical of political institutions, even a familiar conservative campus setting may no longer guarantee an enthusiastic audience.

The GOP may have a strategy for reaching fraternity houses. Whether the young men inside are interested in joining the movement is another question entirely.

👀 Tether has led a $15 million Series A funding round for New York-based Mural, supporting the financial technology company’s development of payment infrastructure for businesses and artificial intelligence agents. Mural plans to use the investment to expand internationally and develop the banking, payment and compliance services needed for software agents to conduct financial transactions.

🔔 Founded in 2022 by former Palantir engineers Sinclair Toffa and Chris Fernandes, the company provides infrastructure that businesses use to manage accounts, payment instructions, identity verification and regulatory requirements across banking networks and blockchains. Its customers include global payroll provider Deel, browser developer Opera and financial technology platform Axexo. Through Mural’s system, businesses can offer accounts holding dollars, local currencies and stablecoins without managing separate financial infrastructure for each payment method.

📌 The company reported processing $2.1 billion in payments for users across 128 countries since introducing its application programming interface in 2025. Payment volume recorded so far in 2026 is nearly six times its total for 2025. Mural has not disclosed the valuation attached to the latest funding round. Fortune reported that the company previously raised $5 million in seed financing in 2022, followed by additional capital from existing backers.
